title: Your Whole Training History, Backfilled Automatically
summary: Switching training apps normally means starting from an empty calendar. HYBRD imports the history you already recorded, so your first week in the app is not your first week of data.
body_markdown:
The real cost of changing training apps is not the subscription. It is the empty calendar. A new app knows nothing about the last year you spent building an aerobic base, so it cannot tell you whether this week is heavy or light, cannot compare today's effort to anything, and cannot build a plan that respects what you can already handle. Most people give up in the first fortnight for exactly this reason.


HYBRD's answer is to import your history rather than wait for you to build a new one. As the in-app tutorial puts it: HYBRD pulls in as much of your training history as possible, regardless of what devices you use, so your training data lives here.


## Import is not the same as sync


This is the distinction that matters and the one most apps blur. Sync means new workouts flow in from today onward. Import means the ones you already did come with you.


Connect Apple Health and HYBRD works backwards through roughly a year of activity, filling it in progressively so you are not stuck waiting on a long history. The same happens on the other side: connecting a provider like Garmin, Strava, WHOOP, Concept2, or Peloton kicks off a backfill of what that account already holds.


The practical effect is that the calendar has depth on day one. Your[Training Score](https://www.hybrd.com/blog/training-score-explained) needs six weeks of load to mean anything, Training State compares your last 7 days to your last 21, and every card in[Trends](https://www.hybrd.com/blog/training-trends-explained) needs a last week to compare this one against. All of those are useless on an empty account and immediately useful on a backfilled one.


## Four colours, one calendar


Imported sessions land on the same calendar as everything else, colour-coded by what they were: cardio, strength, hybrid, and restorative. It sounds cosmetic and it is not. Scroll back three months and the pattern of your training is visible without reading a single label, which is how you notice that your "balanced" block was eleven weeks of cardio with a lift every other Friday.


The calendar also keeps two counters at the top, a dot streak and your workouts in the last 30 days, which is the cheapest consistency check in the app.


## Not to be confused with importing context


HYBRD has a separate feature for pulling in the conversations you have had with ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini about your training, so the coach starts out knowing your goals and history in your own words. That is[importing context](https://www.hybrd.com/import-memory) , and it is a different thing from this.


Backfill brings **workouts** : dates, distances, loads, heart rate, sets. Context import brings **intent** : what you are training for and what you have tried. Doing both is what makes the first plan feel like it was written by someone who already knows you.


## The open-ecosystem argument


Backfill only works because the data is portable in the first place. This is the practical version of the case we made in[the future of fitness is an open ecosystem](https://www.hybrd.com/blog/future-fitness-open-ecosystem) : your training history should be yours, and moving it between tools should not cost you a year of context. An app that cannot import your past is a lock-in mechanism with a training plan attached.


## Where to find it


Settings, then integrations. Connect Apple Health and any providers you use and the backfill starts on its own; it continues in the background, so a long history keeps filling in after you close the app. Connecting more than one provider beyond Apple Health is part of a HYBRD subscription.


## Key Takeaways


- Backfill imports the workouts you already did, rather than only syncing new ones from today
- Apple Health goes back about a year, filling in progressively in the background
- Connecting a provider such as Garmin, Strava, or WHOOP kicks off a backfill of what that account already holds
- It is what makes the six-week Training Score and the 7-versus-21-day Training State useful on day one instead of in two months
- Imported sessions are colour-coded cardio, strength, hybrid, and restorative, so the shape of a past block is readable at a glance
- This is separate from importing your ChatGPT or Claude context: one brings workouts, the other brings intent
